title: Nehushtan: A Lesson in Godly Purity
paragraphs: Nehushtan: A Lesson in Godly Purity
There are things people keep long after God has moved on.

Not because those things are holy.
Because those things are familiar.
That was the tragedy of Nehushtan.

What once served as a sign of God’s mercy became an object of false worship. What once pointed beyond itself became the very thing people bowed to. And that is how impurity often enters a life—not always through obvious rebellion, but through misplaced reverence.

But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Idolatry does not always begin with evil things. Sometimes it begins with gifted things, sacred memories, spiritual experiences, or symbols God once used. Read that again.
In Numbers 21, when Israel sinned against the Lord, fiery serpents came among the people. Death spread through the camp. Then God, in mercy, gave Moses a strange instruction:

“And the Lord said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.”
— Numbers 21:8
And Scripture says:

“And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.”
— Numbers 21:9

The bronze serpent was never the Savior.
It was a sign.

It was never the source of healing.
It was an instrument through which God chose to show mercy.
And for a time, it served its purpose.

But generations later, the people of Judah did something deadly. They took what God had once used and turned it into something God never commanded them to worship. In the days of King Hezekiah, Scripture says:

“He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan.”
— 2 Kings 18:4

That word—Nehushtan—carries the idea of a mere piece of bronze.
Hezekiah stripped away the illusion. He exposed the lie. He called it what it really was.

Not revival.
Not glory.
Not God.
Just bronze.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior, this is where the knife turns inward: how many people today are still burning incense to “Nehushtan”?
Not literally, perhaps. But spiritually? Constantly.

Some worship the memory of a past move of God.
Some worship church tradition more than Christ.
Some worship platforms, preachers, methods, relics, titles, aesthetics, family heritage, or emotional experiences.
Some are devoted to what once helped them encounter truth, but they no longer bow before the living God Himself.
And the Lord is not indifferent to that.

“Thou shalt have no other gods before me.”
— Exodus 20:3

“Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen.”
— 1 John 5:21

Godly purity is not merely avoiding immoral behavior. It is the cleansing of worship. It is the tearing down of everything that competes with the throne of God in the heart. That is why this matters so deeply. Purity is not just about what you stop doing. It is about who alone you bow to.

Here is the deeper danger: religious corruption can look reverent on the outside. Burning incense looked spiritual. It looked sacred. It even involved something connected to biblical history. But sincerity does not sanctify disobedience.

“This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.”
— Matthew 15:8

That is the crisis of Nehushtan.
The form remained.
The fear of God did not.
And maybe that is where some souls are right now.

You still carry the symbol.
You still know the language.
You still preserve the memory.
But the fire of true devotion has been replaced by ritual, nostalgia, or attachment to what God used yesterday.
If this found you, it’s not by accident.
Because the lesson of Nehushtan is not just destruction. It is purification.

King Hezekiah did not negotiate with the idol.
He did not store it in a museum.
He did not rename it and keep it nearby.
He broke it.
That is what repentance does.

“Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.”
— Isaiah 55:7

Repentance is not sentimental.
It is violent against sin.
It is honest about substitutes.
It tears down what steals affection from God.
And this is where the Gospel shines brighter than the brass serpent ever could.
Jesus Himself took that image from Numbers and revealed its ultimate meaning:

“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.”
— John 3:14–15

The bronze serpent pointed forward to Christ.
Nehushtan was a corrupted sign.
Jesus is the spotless Savior.

Where Israel looked and lived physically, sinners now look to Christ and live eternally.
Where idols enslave, Jesus redeems.
Where religion corrupts, Jesus cleanses.
Where sin condemns, Jesus saves.
Because the real problem is deeper than misplaced symbols. The real problem is the sinful heart.

“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
— Romans 3:23

“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
— Romans 6:23
That is why godly purity cannot be achieved by self-effort alone. You do not become clean by smashing one idol while secretly enthroning yourself. You need more than reform. You need redemption.
You need the blood of Jesus.

“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
— Romans 5:8

“In whom we have redemption through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins.”
— Colossians 1:14

This is the call: repent of sin, turn from idols, and trust fully in Jesus Christ. Not in objects. Not in tradition. Not in religious performance. Not in your own strength. Salvation is by grace through faith.

“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast.”
— Ephesians 2:8–9

So ask yourself plainly:
What has become Nehushtan in your life?

What are you protecting that God is calling you to break?
What are you revering that no longer points you to Christ?
What sacred-looking thing has quietly stolen the worship that belongs to God alone?
Read that again.
And here is the mercy of God: when He exposes the idol, He is not trying to ruin you. He is trying to free you.

“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”
— John 8:36
Follow the source.
Bring every idol into the light. Turn to Jesus Christ.
